add_eyes.name: Volkmar Happe (the younger)
add_eyes.role: Lawyer and Schwarzburg-Sondershausen official: district officer (Amtsschösser) of Keula and Ebeleben, court councillor (Hofrat) to Count Christian Günther I from 1623, later director of the consistory; in his thirties and forties during the war
add_eyes.side: Lutheran county of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen (Thuringia), drawn back and forth between Saxon, Swedish and imperial forces
add_eyes.where: Greußen, his birthplace, and the residence town of Sondershausen in northern Thuringia
add_eyes.vantage_label: provincial official recording what the war did to his county
add_eyes.form: chronicle (dated year-by-year entries, revised by the author after the war)
add_eyes.authenticity: Two-volume manuscript 'Chronicon Thuringiae', published online in 2008 by Hans Medick, Norbert Winnige and Andreas Bähr in the series 'Mitteldeutsche Selbstzeugnisse der Zeit des Dreißigjährigen Krieges' (ThULB Jena), cited by folio (e.g. I: 24v). Happe kept entries as events happened but edited the chronicle after the war, so some passages may be reworked. The online edition could not be opened in this session; the entries below rest on folio-cited paraphrases in E. B. Johnson's 2014 University of Georgia thesis and on Medick's work. The calendar is not stated; as a Lutheran territory Schwarzburg used Old Style, so dates are converted on that assumption.
add_eyes.bio: Happe was born at Greußen on 15 November 1587 and spent his career as a lawyer in the service of the Counts of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen. His chronicle sets comets, smallpox, plague, hail and frost beside the passage of armies. He first praised Gustavus Adolphus as a Protestant saviour and grew more bitter as the Swedish troops behaved no better than the imperial ones. He is the official counterpart to Heberle: the same Lutheran reading of the war as God's punishment, but written by a man who sat on the count's council.

sources.title: Volkmar Happe, Chronicon Thuringiae, ed. H. Medick, N. Winnige, A. Bähr (ThULB Jena, 2008), online edition
E. B. Johnson, 'Violence and Retaliation: Civilian Agency in Thuringia during the Thirty Years' War' (MA thesis, University of Georgia, 2014), PDF

add_eyes.name: Vilém Slavata of Chlum and Košumberk
add_eyes.role: Catholic Bohemian nobleman, aged 45; one of the imperial regents (governors) of Bohemia in 1618, later Supreme Chancellor of Bohemia
add_eyes.where: In the council chamber of the Bohemian chancellery, Prague Castle, on 23 May 1618, and then on the slope beneath its window
add_eyes.vantage_label: victim of the act that started the war
add_eyes.authenticity: Slavata's 'Historické spisování' (Historical writings), 14 large books written between 1637 and 1651, covers the Bohemian revolt and the first years of the war, mainly 1608–1619. It is a retrospective work by a victim with every reason to blacken the rebels, written two decades after the event. Its text was not consulted in this session. His entry below is built from standard biographical facts and from an anonymous contemporary eyewitness account of the defenestration (Documenta Bohemica Bellum Tricennale Illustrantia II, 1972; English translation on GHDI). Bohemia used the Gregorian calendar from 1584.
add_eyes.bio: A convert to Catholicism and a hard-line Counter-Reformation administrator, Slavata was hated by the Protestant estates for how he treated Utraquist subjects on his lands. Thrown from the chancellery window with Jaroslav Bořita of Martinic and the secretary Philip Fabricius, he survived, was held by the rebels, and escaped to Saxony about a year later. He returned after White Mountain and spent his old age writing the long history in which he was the wronged party. He is the only eye in this chapter who stood at the war's very first moment.

sources.title: GHDI: The War Begins — The Defenestration of Prague (May 1618), anonymous eyewitness account, trans. E. Yutzy Glebe

add_entries.date_display: Wednesday 23 May 1618 (N.S.; Bohemia used the Gregorian calendar)
add_entries.headline: Thrown from the chancellery window by the Protestant estates
add_entries.digest: After morning Mass the Catholic regents are in the council room when armed Protestant lords push in, demand an answer about the emperor's letter, and accuse Slavata and Martinic of persecuting their fellow believers. The two men are dragged back and forth between the stove and the window. The fingers of Slavata's right hand are beaten until they bleed while he prays for mercy. He goes out in his black velvet coat, after Martinic and before the secretary Fabricius, and rolls further down the slope than either. All three survive the fall of some thirty cubits, which Catholic writers soon called a miracle and the rebels called justice.
add_entries.source_note: Date and sequence from the anonymous contemporary eyewitness account (Documenta Bohemica II, pp. 42–49; GHDI translation). Slavata's own Historické spisování (1637–51) was not consulted, so the digest describes what happened to him rather than his wording.

add_entries.headline: Slavata escapes the rebels and goes into exile
add_entries.digest: Badly injured in the fall and kept under the rebels' control, Slavata gets away about a year after the defenestration and flees to Saxony. The Saxon elector, anxious to stay neutral, sends him on to Passau. He waits there until the imperial victory at White Mountain in November 1620 lets him return to Bohemia.
add_entries.source_note: Wikipedia (Vilém Slavata of Chlum); month and day not found.

add_entries.headline: A terrible comet appears over Thuringia
add_entries.digest: Happe records that a fearful comet showed itself in the heavens and stayed visible for months. Writing with hindsight, he ties it to the war and to all the misfortunes that came after it. About 300 km to the south, Heberle was reading the same star the same way.
add_entries.source_note: Happe, Chronicon Thuringiae I: 24v, as cited and translated in Johnson (2014). Calendar assumed Old Style (Lutheran Schwarzburg).

add_entries.headline: Plague takes his brother's pregnant bride
add_entries.digest: At about six in the morning the plague kills Sibylle Döbler, the young bride of Happe's brother Andreas, and the child she was carrying dies with her. That summer twenty-three people are buried in a single day, and Happe writes that he has never known a sadder year. A heavy frost later the same month adds to the losses. No army is needed for this entry: in the 1620s disease was the war's advance guard.
add_entries.source_note: Happe, Chronicon Thuringiae I: 58r–58v, 59v, 65v, as cited in Johnson (2014).

add_entries.date_display: 1632 (day not given in the source consulted)
add_entries.headline: Pappenheim's soldiers turn Greußen into a home for dragons
add_entries.digest: Happe describes soldiers of Pappenheim's army plundering his home town: women assaulted, people killed, the churches broken open and the place laid waste. He writes that Greußen had become a dwelling for dragons rather than people, a biblical image of desolation. The general who had counted Magdeburg's dead the year before now has his name on Happe's own streets.
add_entries.source_note: Happe, Chronicon Thuringiae I: 258v (with I: 378r), as cited in Johnson (2014); only the year was given there.

add_entries.headline: A fiery light at night, and villagers think Judgment Day has come
add_entries.digest: Around eight in the evening a fiery light is seen over Schernberg. The schoolmaster rings the bells because people think the whole village is on fire, and many believe the Last Judgement has arrived. After years of soldiers burning villages, a light in the night sky was read first as arson and then as the end of the world.
add_entries.source_note: Happe, Chronicon Thuringiae I: 349r–349v, as cited in Johnson (2014) and Medick, 'The Thirty Years' War as Experience and Memory', p. 72.

add_entries.place: Pillau, then the Pomeranian coast near Rügenwalde
add_entries.headline: Shipwrecked on the way to join Gustavus Adolphus
add_entries.digest: Monro ships his men from Pillau to join the Swedish landing in Pomerania. A storm drives the ship off course and wrecks it near Rügenwalde (Darłowo). The soldiers get ashore on improvised floats, and Monro takes the town and castle with local help and holds the area for about nine weeks. His 'First Duty' of Swedish service starts as a survival story rather than a battle.
add_entries.source_note: Monro, His Expedition (1637), Part II, Duty 1 (EEBO-TCP text, quod.lib.umich.edu A07628). He used the Julian calendar.

add_entries.headline: Palm Sunday storm of Frankfurt on the Oder
add_entries.digest: After a morning service, Gustavus orders the brigades to stand ready, and at about five in the afternoon they cross the moat and storm the walls once the cannon fire. Monro's men get in by a sally port, take nine colours and cut the bridge so the garrison cannot escape. Revenge for the imperial massacre at New Brandenburg shapes how the defenders are treated, and Monro stops to condemn the greed of plunder. Five weeks later Magdeburg, which the Swedes failed to relieve, would fall to Tilly.
add_entries.source_note: Monro, His Expedition (1637), Part II, Duty 8 (EEBO-TCP text). Quote: Colonel John Hepburn's words when wounded, as printed by Monro (English, 1637). Palm Sunday Julian 1631 = 3 April O.S. = 13 April N.S.

add_entries.headline: Wounded defending Stralsund against Wallenstein
add_entries.digest: Mackay's regiment, in Danish pay, is sent into Stralsund to help hold the Baltic port against Wallenstein's besieging army. Monro is wounded in the fighting there. The siege fails, and Stralsund's survival brings Sweden into German affairs. In the autumn of that year Monro is made lieutenant colonel.
add_entries.source_note: SSNE database entry 94 (University of St Andrews): 'wounded in action at Stralsund 1628', lieutenant colonel autumn 1628. Monro's own Stralsund duty was not reached in the text consulted, so no day is given.

add_entries.headline: The Friese family reaches safety at Wolmirstedt
add_entries.digest: Three days after a soldier led them out through the burning city to the imperial camp east of the Elbe, the Friese parents and their five children reach Wolmirstedt. From the camp they had watched Magdeburg collapse in a firestorm. They later end up in Altenburg, where the account of their escape was written down.
add_entries.source_note: Volksstimme (Magdeburg), 'Dreißigjähriger Krieg: Die erste Vernichtung', retelling the Friese account; the account itself (printed in Hoffmann's 1911 Magdeburg volume) was not consulted.

add_convergences.label: The comet of November 1618
add_convergences.note: Two Lutherans 300 km apart, a cobbler in Swabia and a court councillor in Thuringia, open their chronicles with the same comet and read it the same way, as God's warning. Neither yet knows that the Prague defenestration six months earlier has started a war; both write it in with hindsight.

add_convergences.label: Spring 1631: two sieges on two rivers
add_convergences.note: While Hagendorf sits in the trenches before Magdeburg on the Elbe, Monro storms Frankfurt on the Oder on Palm Sunday. Gustavus's campaign there was meant in part to draw Tilly off Magdeburg. It failed, and the Scots' revenge for New Brandenburg was soon answered by the Magdeburg massacre.

add_ties.note: Happe records soldiers of Pappenheim's army plundering his home town of Greußen in 1632, a year after Pappenheim counted the dead at Magdeburg.
Not opponents but mirror images: both Lutheran chroniclers read the war as divine punishment and start with the 1618 comet, one from a village bench and one from a count's council.

Arundel's 1636 embassy, which Crowne recorded, went to Ferdinand II, whose regents Slavata had been. It sought to restore the Palatine family whose acceptance of the Bohemian crown followed the defenestration.
In spring 1631 Monro was storming Frankfurt on the Oder while Hagendorf besieged Magdeburg; in September they were in the opposing armies at Breitenfeld.

fix.role: Scottish officer of Mackay's regiment (raised August 1626): captain 1627, lieutenant colonel from autumn 1628, colonel from 1632; in Danish, then Swedish, service
fix.authenticity: Monro, His Expedition with the Worthy Scots Regiment called Mac-Keyes (London, 1637) is a genuine contemporary publication, arranged as numbered 'duties' (campaign narratives) each followed by an 'observation' (moral and military reflection). Dates are Old Style. The EEBO-TCP transcription was consulted for Part I (Danish service, to the retreat to Assens) and for the opening duties of Part II (Swedish service, August 1630 to April 1631). His Breitenfeld chapter was not reached, so that entry remains approximate. It was written up for publication some years after the events, from memory and notes.

fix.role: Boy of about twelve, one of five children of a former Magdeburg town clerk (Stadtschreiber)
fix.authenticity: The Friese account of the family's escape was printed with the account of the preacher Christoph Thodänus in F. W. Hoffmann's 1911 volume on Magdeburg's destruction, and it is the climax of the ZDF/Terra X series. Sources differ on who wrote it: ZDF and Prisma present the twelve-year-old Daniel as the witness, while a Volksstimme retelling says the father wrote down the family's experiences after reaching Altenburg. It is a retrospective family narrative, not a diary. The original text was not consulted here; details come from those two press retellings.
fix.bio: The Friese account sees the sack from an attic. The father smashed the family's stove, doors and furniture with an axe so the house would look already plundered, and bought off two groups of soldiers with money, pearls, food and his best coat. A third soldier found them hiding and raised a hammer, then relented when the youngest boy, Christian, offered his pocket money; the man had sons of his own. For a promised 200 thaler he led the family through the burning streets to the imperial camp.

fix.place: The family house and attic, Magdeburg, then the streets to the imperial camp east of the Elbe
fix.headline: Hiding in the attic, a boy's pocket money and a soldier's mercy
fix.digest: The Friese family has already bought off two groups of soldiers with money, pearls, food and the father's best coat, and he has smashed the stove and doors so the house looks already looted. They hide in the attic with their five children until a soldier chasing a neighbour finds them and raises a spiked hammer. The youngest boy holds out his pocket money, and the soldier, who has sons of his own, lowers the weapon. For a promise of 200 thaler he walks the family through the burning streets to the camp across the Elbe.
fix.source_note: Volksstimme retelling of the Friese account (and ZDF/Prisma for Daniel's age). Date and content agree; authorship (son or father) is uncertain, and the original text was not consulted.

updates.why: Concrete content now confirmed from a press retelling of the account; the date is the sack itself.

fix.authenticity: Two manuscripts survive in the library of Teplá (Tepl) abbey: a Latin 'Diarium, in quo Triplex Rebellio…' (Cod. 62), headed with the date 20 May 1631, and a German 'Diarium, in welchem die Tragoedia…' (Cod. 85). The German version was edited by Ph. Klimesch in Archiv für Kunde österreichischer Geschichtsquellen 16 (1856). Extracts appeared as Die Katastrophe von Magdeburg 1631: Auszug aus dem Tagebuch, ed. Onno Klopp (Freiburg: Herder, 1874, 78 pp.). Written in Cologne in 1633, it is considered the only contemporary account from the Catholic-imperial side and is used in the dispute over who started the fire (the NDB article on Falkenberg thinks the Swedish commander likely ordered it). NDB says 'the Swedes' drove Bandhauer out in 1631 without making clear whether he was expelled from the city itself.

sources.title: Die Katastrophe von Magdeburg 1631, ed. O. Klopp (1874), library record
